title: What do 96 and 275 have in common?
description: Ninety six and two hundred and seventy five are written as primes, one above the other, and no prime sits in both rows. The factor one is the only common factor, so it is also the highest. Keeko's doubt, that the numbers have no common factor at all, is answered by dividing each number by one.
teaching_notes: One idea: when no prime sits in both factorisations, the only common factor, and so the HCF, is one. Watch for students who say such numbers have no common factor.

source: Find the common factors and the HCF of 96 and 275.
video_script.why: The child has found shared groups of primes and now meets a pair of numbers with no shared prime.
video_script.substitution: If no prime sits in both factorisations, no group is shared, so the only common factor is the factor one.
video_script.anchor: Ninety six and two hundred and seventy five written as primes, one above the other.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says there is no common factor because the rows share no prime. But one divides every number exactly, so one is always a common factor.
video_script.payoff_line: The highest common factor is one.

final_answer.value: The only common factor is 1, so the HCF is 1
final_answer.spoken: the only common factor is one, so the highest common factor is one

hold_back: The only common factor is 1, so the HCF is 1
maths_rules: 96 has the primes 2 and 3; 275 has the primes 5 and 11. No prime is in both.
So no group of primes is shared, and the only common factor is 1. The highest is 1.
Slip: 1 divides every number exactly (96 / 1 = 96, 275 / 1 = 275), so 1 is always a common factor.
video_script.design: One idea: no shared prime means the only common factor is one. Assumes prime factorisation. Wrong idea: no common factor at all. The two factorisations stay on the board all video.
